paragraphs.text: Lesson 27, apologizing and expressing regret.
In yesterday's lesson you learned how to argue and swear in English, but after having
an argument or fight, it's important to apologize in order to maintain a good relationship.
This lesson will teach you about the different ways to say you're sorry and accept responsibility
for what you did wrong.
Kim and Nathan are a married couple.
They had a big fight earlier in the day because Kim booked flights to visit her parents during
their vacation, but Nate had been making other plans to travel with friends.
Now listen to their conversation as they make amends.
Kim, I just wanted to apologize for yelling at you earlier.
Well you should be sorry.
I've been under a lot of stress at work, but that's no excuse.
I shouldn't have lost my temper.
Look, don't worry about it.
I'd like to apologize too.
I definitely should have checked with you before making plans for our vacation.
It's alright.
Next time I'll make sure we're on the same page about decisions like this.
It's partially my fault too.
I've been so busy that we haven't even really had time to talk lately.
I understand.
You know, sometimes I wish I hadn't taken this job.
It's turning out to be more demanding than I expected.
I'm sure it'll get easier once you learn the ropes.
What do you want to do about our vacation though?
If only I hadn't bought non-refundable tickets.
That's okay.
We'll go visit your family this year and next year we'll plan a trip together.
Conversation vocabulary and phrases.
The basic way to apologize is to say I'm sorry or I want to apologize or I'd like to
apologize.
That's more formal.
You can also add the word for and then describe exactly why you are apologizing.
For example, I'm sorry for yelling at you.
I'm sorry for using your computer without asking.
I want to apologize for losing my temper.
I'd like to apologize for missing the deadline.
For very minor mistakes like bumping into someone, you can use these phrases.
Oops, sorry.
Sorry about that.
Excuse me.
Say, excuse me when you cough, burp, fart, blow your nose or make another bodily noise in
public.
If you did something very bad and you want to apologize even more strongly, you can say,
I'm really sorry.
I'm so sorry.
Please accept my sincere apology.
That phrase is very formal, only to be used in professional situations.
I can't express how sorry I am.
Accepting responsibility.
When apologizing, it can be helpful to show that you recognize what you did wrong.
Here are some phrases for expressing your role in the problem.
It was my fault.
I messed up.
I know I let you down.
It was wrong of me too.
I should have or I shouldn't have.
Use these phrases to say what you wish you had done differently.
For example, I should have called to tell you I'd be late.
I shouldn't have taken your CD without asking.
I accept full responsibility.
That's more formal.
My behavior was inexcusable.
That's also very formal.
Promising to do better.
It's also common to include a promise in your apology using will or won't.
For example, sorry about the spill.
I'll clean it up.
I'm sorry for breaking your calculator.
I'll buy you another one.
I apologize for the mistake.
I'll be more careful next time.
I'd like to apologize for being late.
It won't happen again.
Asking for forgiveness.
Sometimes people end an apology by asking the other person to forgive.
For example, please don't be angry at me.
Please don't hold it against me.
Will you forgive me?
Responding to an apology.
There are several ways to respond to an apology depending on the situation and the seriousness
of the problem.
You can say, that's okay.
It's alright.
Don't worry about it.
No problem.
No harm done.
Say no harm done to emphasize that there's no major damage resulting from the person's
mistake.
It happens.
Say, it happens when the other person has made a mistake that is common and happens frequently
to everyone.
I understand.
For more serious problems you can add these phrases.
They emphasize the fact that you consider the problem resolved and you don't want it to
affect your relationship in the future.
Here are the phrases.
Let's forget about it.
We'll say no more about it.
We'll consider the matter closed.
I forgive you.
You're forgiven.
Unfortunately when you apologize the other person might still be angry and not want to accept
the apology.
Here are some examples of angry rejections of apologies.
I'm sorry for the way I treated you yesterday.
You should be.
I'd like to apologize for the late delivery.
Well, that's not good enough.
I'd like a refund too.
Sorry about the loud music last night.
Don't do it again.
Or don't let it happen again.
You can use a variation of this last phrase together with one of the other phrases when
you do want to accept the apology, but you also want to warn the other person that future
mistakes will not be tolerated.
For example, it's all right.
Just don't let it happen again, okay?
In the conversation we also see four different ways to express regret.
I should have and I shouldn't have.
For example, I should have studied harder for that test.
I was pretty unprepared.
I saw a beautiful sunset yesterday.
I should have taken a picture.
I shouldn't have left my umbrella at home.
It's starting to rain now.
I have a stomach ache.
I shouldn't have eaten so much at the buffet.
Most native speakers actually pronounce these expressions like should of or should of and
shouldn't of or shouldn't of, but the correct way to write it is always should have and shouldn't
have.
So remember this when you're writing in English.
Another way to express regret is to say I regret plus the ing form of the verb.
For example, I regret dropping out of school.
It was a big mistake.
I regret waiting until I was an adult to start learning another language.
I regret not studying abroad when I had the chance.
I regret not staying in touch with my childhood friends.
When talking about things you wish were different in the past, always use the ing form of the
verb after regret.
Using the word regret is a bit more formal.
In spoken English we usually use the next structure.
I wish I had and I wish I hadn't.
I wish is followed by the past perfect to express regret.
For example, I wish I'd started taking dance lessons years ago.
I'm stuck in traffic.
I wish I'd taken the train instead of the bus.
I wish I hadn't broken up with my high school boyfriend, but I was young and immature.
I wish I hadn't drunk that whole bottle of wine yesterday.
Now I have a terrible hangover.
Finally we have the phrase if only plus the past perfect.
This phrase is often used as an exclamation.
For example, if only I'd invested in Apple computers twenty years ago, if I had I'd be
rich today.
If only I'd known you were coming, I would have made dinner.
If only I hadn't been so shy in college, I probably would have had a lot more fun.
I couldn't sleep at all last night if only I hadn't watched that horror movie before going
to bed.
If only plus the past perfect is often followed by imagining what would have happened if your
action in the past had been different, as in the first three example sentences.
You've finished lesson 27.
Today's speaking task is to leave a message telling me one thing you had to apologize for
and one or two regrets you have.
Describe this situation and try to use some of the phrases from the lesson.
Click on the link in the lesson text to record your message.
